newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FERC ponders natgas pipeline oversight role.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FERC ponders natgas pipeline oversight role.

text.p: U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission Thursday heard from various voices of the natural gas industry as it pondered how much market power pipelines have and the commission's role in increasing competitiveness in the industry.

"In virtually all the issues we're discussing the issue of monopoly power keeps raising its head. The question is to what extent do pipelines have monopoly power," Commissioner William Massey said at a conference the commission held on the future of the gas industry.
Pipeline operators argued that they are not monopolies because most areas of the country have excess pipeline capacity, and so should have a freer hand to negotiate rates and terms.
"If they are (monopolies), we've been working awfully hard to cut costs and stay competitive," Larry Hall, of the Interstate Natural Gas Association of America and president of KN Energy Inc, said.
But gas producers, marketers and end users said pipelines are natural monopolies and said FERC should continue to rein them in.
"We would caution against negotiated rates and conditions without competition," Judd Miller, Exxon Corp vice president for natural gas, said.

Speaking for the Natural Gas Supply Association, Miller said if negotiated rates and terms were used, there must be recourse service "that reasonably approximates the negotiated service," as well as full disclosure of negotiated terms.

Edward Grenier, speaking for large industrial gas consumers, said it was "wishing thinking" to believe that recourse rates would restrain pipelines' monopoly power, and said "a potpourri of rate designs" would interfere with the "seamless web" of service the FERC was seeking.
George Watson, president of TransCanada Pipelines, suggested the commission consider market-based pipeline rates that would reflect whether an area was over- or under-built.

Stephen Bergstrom, president of Natural Gas Clearinghouse, representing gas marketers, said the commission should focus its resources on electricity restructuring instead of "exotic new schemes to increase profitability of pipelines."
He suggested independent systems operators could be used to "eliminate opportunities for pipelines to discriminate."
The commission also heard different views on how to increase competition behind the citygate, and what FERC's role should be in that.

Ruth Kretschmer, of the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners, said local distribution companies will resist competition because "the playing field is not level in their own states," and said state legislatures must act first.
Federal regulators should not try to impose a single model for states to follow, and states -- not FERC -- should set rates at the LDC level, Kretschmer said.

"Local distribution companies are moving toward full competition, but they will implement cometition differently, reflecting different state policy choices," Richard Terry, of the American Gas Association and chairman of Peoples Gas Light and Coke Co of Chicago, said.
INGAA urged a push for increased competition among LDCs, and said LDCs that agree to unbundle services should qualify for uncapped rates at all their interstate delivery points.
